results.markdown:
Title: Salon advertising: fill your appointment book

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/salon-advertising-growing-your-beauty-business

Published Time: 2026-04-09T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Salon advertising fills the appointment book when people nearby see your work and can book in one tap. Pair search ads, which reach people already looking for a cut or color, with social and streaming TV ads that show your work.

Send all of it to one booking page, and start with a budget you can keep running for several weeks.

## Where new salon clients come from

Salon demand is local, and most clients won’t drive across a metro area for a trim, so a new client usually lives or works within a short distance of your chairs. When someone searches for a salon, Google decides which businesses to show. Roz Hair’s [salon guide to Google Business Profile fixes](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqQEB6zswFVldt3iqN5H9tIifR93S4Bns7BNKaPiNITX57z_dGI-6Y-IkvlqB7yPdVE-WqZiG626rkZidXHLLi-_Ej4bAoHwCsSbD5UrvMXAjzi9jF-yQlObdvU1Dau0P_Jmxo0knkRDWcL6AdzZQ6VHOKaKmXKKaw-YVIgEo61gVEZU5BUWGvorreDYwM7_UB52hZ82Quoj-O_68VXzAaSomd-dEBxwwf5Ix) summarizes Google’s local ranking guidance: local results depend mainly on three things, relevance, distance and prominence. Relevance means your profile matches the service searched. Distance means how close you are to the searcher. Prominence means how well known and well reviewed you are.

![Image 1: Woman checks her phone outside a neighborhood hair salon while stylists work inside](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/1c3706ca683e0107e7dc0ae6402f2e088cbba8dc8735b5c215177584d8f0c0a2.jpg)

The Google Business Profile is the free part of that picture. A complete, active profile has the right business category, every service listed, current hours, recent photos of your work and your space, and ongoing genuine reviews. The Local Gem’s [Google Business Profile guide for salons](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESfgHrOzAVL0r7GwWKPw75TlhnsTuuHcrzSC9HWFqnU_Z_OIHA2AbRUyirAS6hArgqbtseVzoccIVt_1BVVsi4ypfBJTJWDvS6SmRV0MxfPI50soDm9PVN29jjN-_6ZcfJnUvK3-pIjKXzkqoLues3PkdK6V6_JRbLVHMqZ9KEpw) points out that the profile costs nothing to set up or maintain. It also says salons that complete it and keep posting and collecting reviews usually see better local visibility within 4 to 8 weeks.

That free visibility is groundwork. You manage it yourself, and Adwave doesn’t run it for you. It does affect how well paid ads perform. Someone who sees your Instagram ad or streaming TV spot will often search your name before booking. If they find a sparse profile with three reviews from 2022, you lose some of what the ad earned. Get the profile in order first, then use paid campaigns to reach people who haven’t found you yet.

## Choosing advertising channels for a salon

Search, social and streaming TV each bring a salon a different kind of client. Search catches people who are looking right now. Social shows your work to people who weren’t looking. Streaming TV makes your name familiar across the neighborhood. Most salons need a mix, and the right mix depends on whether your chairs are empty this week or you’re building a client base for next season. Our page on [running TV, search and social from one budget](https://adwave.com/solutions/omnichannel) shows how that mix works in a single campaign.

The budget column shows the daily amount at which each channel becomes available in an Adwave campaign, based on [Adwave’s current published pricing](https://adwave.com/pricing/).

| Channel | Salon job it does | Best for | Available in Adwave from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google Search | Reaches people searching for a service near them, such as balayage near me | Filling open slots this week | $30/day |
| Facebook and Instagram | Shows before-and-after photos and short videos to nearby people by age and interest | New clients who choose a stylist by looking at their work | $30/day |
| YouTube and Google Demand Gen | Video and image ads across Google’s network | Broad local reach with video | $30/day |
| Streaming TV | Puts a 15- or 30-second spot on the living room screen in your area | Local familiarity, launches, new locations | $30/day |
| Mobile web and apps | Image ads on sites and apps people use every day | Repeat exposure at low cost | $30/day |
| Reddit | Ads in local and interest communities | Younger, research-minded clients | about $35/day |

Instagram and Facebook carry most salon work because clients pick a salon by looking at results. Search is the closest thing to a ready-to-book client, and it is available from the same $30/day floor as social and streaming TV. Streaming TV costs less than most salon owners expect, and a TV spot gives a salon the kind of presence that word of mouth usually takes years to build. Our page on [streaming TV for salons and barbershops](https://adwave.com/industries/beauty-wellness/hair-salons/tv-advertising-salons-barbershops) covers that channel in more depth.

TikTok is live and opt-in in Adwave, starting from [$91 per day](https://adwave.com/pricing/) once you turn it on in Customize and connect your TikTok account.

## What to put in salon ads

Salon advertising sells a visible result, so the creative should show results. The ideas below are example guidance for building ads. They are not measured outcomes.

![Image 2: Stylist reveals a client's new balayage in the mirror while a camera records the moment](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/4a69c170921ebb3d6787412dcc677d36ef3db2f16240af7c89d653002de1cfc2.jpg)

A color correction or a big cut shown side by side, before and after, explains your skill faster than any headline, and on TV and vertical video the chair-turn reveal does the same job. Many clients follow a person more than a brand, so a short clip of a stylist introducing their specialty, curly cuts or blonding, for example, gives a new client a reason to pick a name on your booking page. Choose one service with a price or a clear reason to book rather than a general welcome to the salon: an ad for new-client gloss with any color service does more work than a vague invitation. End every ad with the next step, such as book online or see open times this week, and make sure the link goes to a page where booking is actually possible. Use real photos of your own interior, team and storefront, not stock images, since clients want to know what the room looks like before they sit in it.

Keep every ad consistent with your website. Adwave reads your site for offers and photos when it builds a campaign, so the ads reflect what’s actually there. If your site still lists last year’s prices or a stylist who has moved on, fix that first, because a client who clicks an ad and finds different information on the site is less likely to book. For TV specifically, see what works in [TV spots for salons and spas](https://adwave.com/industries/beauty-wellness/hair-salons/tv-advertising-salons-spas-beauty).

## How much salons spend on advertising

There’s no official salon benchmark, but several published reference points give a reasonable range. The most common rule of thumb is 5 to 15% of revenue. Zoca’s [line-by-line salon marketing cost breakdown](https://zoca.com/post/how-much-does-salon-marketing-cost-per-month) (September 2026) traces that figure to Grow A Salon and notes it comes with no derivation. For a salon taking in $15,000 a month, the rule works out to $750 to $2,250 a month.

[Boulevard’s salon budget examples](https://www.joinblvd.com/blog/salon-budget-examples) list monthly marketing ranges of $150 to $750 for a smaller operation and $500 to $1,500 for a larger one, covering social media, email, print and paid ads. Zoca’s same breakdown cites a LocaliQ survey of more than 300 small business owners from February 2026, in which 52% had a monthly marketing budget under $1,000. It also cites ClicksGeek’s published agency retainer ranges, which start at $1,000 to $3,000 a month before any ad spend.

Those figures help with planning. At $30 a day, 30 active days of media comes to $900, which sits inside Boulevard’s larger range and near the low end of the 5 to 15% rule for a $15,000-a-month salon. At $75 a day, 30 days comes to $2,250, nearer the top of that range. Pick the amount you can keep running for several weeks without pulling it in a slow month, since a campaign that runs briefly and stops doesn’t show you much. For broader cost context across channels, see our [local advertising cost guide](https://adwave.com/resources/local-advertising-cost-guide-2026).

## Running salon ads across channels with Adwave

Adwave builds the ads from your salon’s website and runs them across TV, search, social and the web from one daily budget. The setup takes five steps:

### [What Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists Do](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-2)

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide haircutting, hairstyling, and other services related to personal appearance.

### [Work Environment](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-3)

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists work mostly in barbershops or salons. Most are full time, although part-time work is common. Work schedules may vary and often include evenings and weekends.

### [How to Become a Barber, Hairstylist, or Cosmetologist](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-4)

All states require barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists to be licensed. To qualify for a license, candidates typically must graduate from a state-approved barber or cosmetology program and pass an exam.

### [Pay](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-5)

The median hourly wage for barbers was $18.37 in May 2025.

The median hourly wage for hairdressers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists was $17.21 in May 2025.

### [Job Outlook](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-6)

Overall employment of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists is projected to grow 7 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations.

About 80,300 openings for barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists are projected each year, on average, over the decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire.

### [State & Area Data](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-7)

Explore resources for employment and wages by state and area for barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists.

### [Similar Occupations](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-8)

Compare the job duties, education, job growth, and pay of barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists with similar occupations.

### [More Information, Including Links to O*NET](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#tab-9)

Learn more about barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists by visiting additional resources, including O*NET, a source on key characteristics of workers and occupations.

## What Barbers, Hairstylists, and Cosmetologists Do[About this section](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#TB_inline?height=325&width=325&inlineId=about-what-they-do)

![Image 1: Barbers, hairdressers, and cosmetologists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/images/2711.jpg)

Hairstylists provide hair styling and beauty services.

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide haircutting, hairstyling, and other services related to personal appearance.

### Duties

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists typically do the following:

*   Inspect and analyze hair, scalp, and skin to recommend services or treatment
*   Discuss hairstyle options
*   Shampoo, color, lighten, and condition hair
*   Chemically change hair texture
*   Cut, dry, and style hair
*   Trim facial hair
*   Receive payments from client
*   Clean and disinfect all tools and work areas

Barbers, hairstylists, and cosmetologists provide hair and other services to enhance clients’ appearance. Common tools may include combs and hairbrushes, clippers and scissors, straight razors, blow dryers, and curling and flat irons. They also may keep records of products used and services provided to clients, such as hair color, hair treatment, and clipper setting.

Those who operate their own barbershop or salon have managerial duties that may include hiring, supervising, and firing workers. They also may keep business and inventory records, order supplies, and arrange for advertising.

**_Barbers_** shampoo, cut, and style hair, mostly for male clients. They also may fit hairpieces, provide facials, trim beards and mustaches, and offer facial and head shaving. Depending on the state in which they work, some barbers are licensed to bleach, color, and highlight hair and to offer permanent-wave services.

**_Hairstylists_****_and cosmetologists_** offer a wide range of hair services, such as shampooing, cutting, coloring, and styling. They often provide consultation and advise clients on how to care for their hair at home. Some also clean and style wigs and hairpieces.

Hairstylists and cosmetologists also provide facial and scalp treatments, makeup analysis, and skincare and nail services. In addition, some recommend hair care or skincare products. For more information about workers who specialize in skincare treatment or in fingernail and toenail services, see the profiles for [skincare specialists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/skincare-specialists.htm) or [manicurists and pedicurists](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/manicurists-and-pedicurists.htm), respectively.

## Work Environment[About this section](https://www.bls.gov/ooh/personal-care-and-service/barbers-hairstylists-and-cosmetologists.htm#TB_inline?height=325&width=325&inlineId=about-working-environment)

results.title: Tips to improve your local ranking on Google
results.markdown:
Title: Tips to improve your local ranking on Google

URL Source: https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091

Markdown Content:
[Manage your business](https://business.google.com/?skipLandingPage=true&gmbsrc=ww-ww-et-gs-z-gmb-v-z-h~bhc-core-u|mybb)

When a customer searches for a business or place near their location, they’ll find local results on Google Maps and Search. For example, a customer might find local places near them if they search for “Italian restaurant” on their phone. Google tries to show customers the kind of nearby business they’d like to visit.

You can use your Business Profile to improve your business’s local ranking. [Learn more about how Google sources business information for search results](https://support.google.com/business/answer/2721884).

[How to improve your local ranking on Google](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WpCeu4ezaeI)

## Verify your business

This tells Google that you’re authorized to represent the business, so it's more likely to show up in search results. [Learn how to verify your business on Google](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7107242).

## [](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091)Keep your business information up-to-date

Businesses with complete and accurate info are more likely to show up in local search results. If your business info isn’t accurate, your Business Profile might not show up for relevant searches in your area.[Learn how to edit your Business Profile](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3039617).

Make sure your business info is as complete as possible in your Business Profile. This helps customers know what you do, where you are, and when they can visit. Provide information like:

*   Your full address, if your business has a location that customers can visit. [Learn how to manage your business address](https://support.google.com/business/answer/2853879).
*   Your business hours, including [special store hours](https://support.google.com/business/answer/6303076).[Learn how to edit your hours](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3039617#hours).
*   What kind of business you are.[Learn how to manage your business category](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7249669).
*   Other details such as parking or Wi-Fi availability. [Learn how to manage your business attributes](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9049526).

## Respond to reviews

When you reply to customer reviews, it shows that you value their feedback. Positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out.

*   [Learn how to manage customer reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/3474050).
*   [Learn more tips to get more Google reviews](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7035772).

## Add photos & videos

You can show customers what you offer and tell the story of your business with photos and videos. [Learn how to manage photos or videos for your Business Profiles](https://support.google.com/business/answer/6103862).

## Add in-store products

**Important:** This is available only for retail businesses in eligible countries or regions.

If you have a retail store, you can show your in-store products on your Business Profile. When you do this, your in-store products might show in local search results and customers can find out what’s in stock. [Learn how to showcase in-store products](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9934993).

## [](https://support.google.com/business/answer/7091)Understand factors that determine local ranking

**Important:** There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google. We do our best to keep the search algorithm details confidential to make the ranking system as fair as possible for everyone.

Local results are mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity. Together, these factors help Google find the best match for customers’ searches.

### Relevance

Relevance is how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for. To help Google better understand your business and match it to relevant searches, provide complete and detailed business info.

### Distance

Distance refers to how far each business is from the customer who’s searching. If a customer doesn’t share where they are, Google uses what it knows about their location.

### Prominence

Prominence means how well-known a business is. Prominent places are more likely to show up in search results. This factor’s also based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have. More reviews and positive ratings can help your business’s local ranking.

## Related resources

*   [Manage your business information](https://support.google.com/business/topic/4596687)
*   [Understand your Business Profile performance & insights](https://support.google.com/business/answer/9918094)

results.title: Ad frequency: how often people should see your ad
results.markdown:
Title: Ad frequency: how often people should see your ad

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/ad-frequency-small-business

Published Time: 2026-11-09T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Ad frequency has no single right number, but the research points to a range. Meta’s brand-lift analysis found a cap of 2 impressions per person per week captured 95% of the potential purchase-intent lift. A CTV study found purchase intent fell as one viewer’s exposures in a session climbed toward six.

Start with a modest weekly cap and adjust when fatigue signals appear.

Ad frequency is the average number of times one person sees your ad during a set period, usually a day, a week or the length of a campaign. If 1,000 people saw your ad 3,000 times in a week, your weekly frequency is 3. Because it is an average, some people saw the ad once and others saw it six or seven times.

A frequency cap is the ceiling: the most times the platform will show your ad to one person in that period. Before serving an ad, the platform checks whether that person has reached the cap and skips them if they have. Many platforms also offer a second control. [Epom’s guide to ad frequency](https://epom.com/blog/dsp/ad-frequency-best-practices) separates the cap, which limits how many times, from recency, which sets the minimum gap between views. Improvado gives a programmatic example of a recency cap: one impression per hour.

Frequency is counted in impressions, and an impression is not the same as a view. [Improvado’s frequency capping glossary](https://improvado.io/blog/understanding-frequency-capping) defines an impression as each time an ad is displayed on a screen, whether or not the person noticed it. Your reported frequency can therefore run higher than the number of times someone actually paid attention, and that is one reason the right number varies by format.

## How frequency works on TV, CTV and social

How much control you have depends on how the channel is bought. Traditional linear TV is sold by time slot and program. [Amazon Ads’ linear TV guide](https://advertising.amazon.com/library/guides/linear-tv-advertising) describes advertisers buying commercial time based on expected viewership, with ads running in scheduled program breaks. You choose the shows and dayparts, but you cannot limit how often one household sees your spot. Streaming TV runs on internet-connected devices, and Amazon Ads notes that these platforms add tools such as completion rates and frequency caps.

![Image 1: Woman on a couch at night holding a phone while a television plays in front of her](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/28d1108883e13878d943344747274317731433efff0b1582443c1a3eb0634236.jpg)

| Channel | How you control frequency | What to know |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear TV (broadcast, cable, satellite) | Indirectly, through the programs, dayparts and number of spots you buy | No per-person cap; frequency is estimated from ratings |
| Streaming TV (CTV) | Per-viewer or per-household caps where the platform offers them | Caps apply within the platform or buying route you use |
| Facebook and Instagram | A target frequency (impressions per person per week) or a frequency cap, set at campaign or ad set level | Campaign-level and ad set-level controls can’t be combined |
| Google display and programmatic | Hard impression caps per day, week or month; some platforms add lifetime and recency caps | Granularity depends on the platform |

Every cap stops at the edge of one platform. Improvado gives an example: a cap of 3 per day on Google and 3 per day on Facebook can still mean 6 impressions a day for the same person. Neither platform knows about the other, so cross-channel frequency is something you have to estimate yourself. For more detail on streaming TV specifically, see [our CTV frequency guide](https://adwave.com/resources/ctv-ad-frequency-how-many-times).

## What research says about effective frequency

Effective frequency is the number of exposures one person needs within a period before an ad produces the response you want. The [Universal Marketing Dictionary’s definition](https://marketing-dictionary.org/e/effective-frequency/) rests on the assumption that the first few exposures may have little effect and the message starts to influence people only after more of them.

The idea has a long and somewhat shaky history. In [a chapter on what effective frequency means today](https://sk.sagepub.com/book/edvol/the-advertising-business/chpt/what-does-effective-frequency-mean-today), advertising researcher John Philip Jones argues that it is “rooted not so much in research as in common sense.” He notes that Michael Naples’s 1979 book gave the practice academic respectability, but its strongest support came from Colin McDonald’s work, which Jones calls “merely a small-scale experiment” done years earlier in another country. Be skeptical of any single magic number, including the popular rule that people must see an ad three times.

Newer platform research is more useful because it measures specific outcomes. [Meta’s effective frequency study](https://www.facebook.com/business/news/insights/effective-frequency-reaching-full-campaign-potential) found that lift in both ad recall and purchase intent rose with frequency, but at different rates:

*   A cap of 1 per week captured up to 80% of the total potential lift in ad recall.
*   Recall lift slowed sharply after a cap of 1 per week, while purchase-intent lift didn’t start to slow until close to 1.5 per week.
*   A cap of 2 per week captured 95% of the total potential purchase-intent lift.

Meta reads this as support for the idea that bigger behavior changes, such as intent to buy, need more exposures than simple recall.

Streaming TV research shows what happens when frequency goes too high. An MNTN CTV study, reported by Epom, found recall rose from about 64% after one view to 92% after six in a single session, while purchase intent fell 16% over the same range and brand affinity slipped. Taken together, these findings suggest recall is a poor guide to frequency: it keeps climbing after the measures that lead to sales have started to decline.

## Starting caps by channel

Epom has published suggested starting caps per user per week. They are one practitioner’s starting points, not industry rules or measured results, and they are useful mainly as a first setting you then test.

| Channel | Suggested starting cap (per user per week) | Epom’s reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CTV / streaming TV | 4 to 6 per viewer | Ads interrupt the show and few creatives are usually in rotation |
| Facebook and Instagram Feed | 3 to 5 | Fatigue commonly sets in around 6 to 7 on a single creative |
| Facebook and Instagram Stories and Reels | 2 to 4 | Higher-attention format with lower tolerance than Feed |
| Programmatic online video | About 10 | Holds attention, but skippable formats fatigue faster |
| Display, prospecting | 15 to 25 | Banner blindness means people tolerate more exposures |
| Display, retargeting | 10 to 15 (about 3 a day at most) | A smaller pool of people gets overexposed quickly |

The Meta Feed range sits above the 2 per week that Meta’s own brand-lift work found efficient for purchase intent, which is why Epom also notes Meta’s data pointing to about 2 per week for awareness. If your goal is a booked appointment or a sale, the lower end is a sensible place to begin. Our guides to [Facebook advertising for small businesses](https://adwave.com/resources/facebook-advertising-for-small-business) and [display ads for small businesses](https://adwave.com/resources/display-advertising-small-business) cover those channels beyond frequency.

Ad fatigue happens when people see the same ad so often that it stops working. [Criteo’s ad fatigue guide](https://www.criteo.com/blog/ad-fatigue-how-to-detect-and-prevent-it/) lists warning signs worth checking weekly:

![Image 2: Bored man looking away from a television and reaching for the remote](https://media.wavefront.adwave-apps.com/ws/ws_adwave/8b5846d3052b24a743cf36127f0c1d8480a3b7a5cd3047739d25e369b5f989b1.jpg)

*   Click-through rate falls while impressions hold flat or rise.
*   Cost per click, cost per thousand impressions or cost per acquisition rises with no clear change in the market.
*   Frequency keeps climbing while engagement drops.
*   One creative takes a large share of the spend but underperforms the campaign’s average click-through rate.
*   The same people see the same message several times in a short window, which is common in retargeting.

[Keen Decision Systems’ ad fatigue guide](https://keends.com/blog/ad-fatigue/) adds two more: unique reach that plateaus while impressions keep piling up, and more negative feedback such as skips or hides. Criteo stresses that combined signals matter more than any one metric. A dip in click-through rate on its own could be seasonal. Falling clicks plus rising costs plus rising frequency is a much clearer warning.
